high_priority_articles.title: UK weighs tariffs on Chinese EVs as EU trade rules loom - fleetpoint.org
high_priority_articles.summary: UK weighs tariffs on Chinese EVs as EU trade rules loom  fleetpoint.org
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Britain is considering tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as the rapid growth of Chinese-owned brands intensifies pressure on the UK automotive industry.
According to reports, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds is drawing up options for additional duties on Chinese vehicle imports. The move follows concerns that heavily subsidised Chinese manufacturers could be “dumping” vehicles into the UK market.
No tariffs have yet been announced. A UK government spokesperson told
: “We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector’s and UK’s national interests.”
The timing is significant for fleet operators. Chinese-owned brands are gaining market share rapidly, while the European Union is developing new measures designed to strengthen domestic automotive manufacturing and reduce reliance on Chinese supply chains.
Chinese cars surge in UK market
The strength of Chinese manufacturers in Britain was underlined by September’s new car registrations.
The SMMT reported 350,518 new cars registered during September, up 12.1% year on year. Battery electric registrations reached a record 99,199, up 36.3%, while plug-in hybrid registrations rose 55.7% to 59,563.
Chinese-owned brands accounted for 27.5% of the September market, according to analysis of the SMMT figures. That means more than one in four new cars registered during the crucial September plate-change month came from a Chinese-owned manufacturer. The year-to-date share has exceeded 21%.
BYD alone registered 20,140 cars in September, giving it a 5.75% market share. Chery recorded 9,788 registrations, while Chinese-owned brands including MG and Jaecoo also performed strongly.
The Jaecoo 7 was particularly notable. It became Britain’s best-selling new car in September, with more than 15,000 registrations according to SMMT data reported by the automotive press.
For fleet managers, the significance goes beyond brand recognition. Chinese manufacturers are increasingly competing through competitive pricing, extensive equipment levels and rapidly expanding dealer networks. They are also helping push down the cost of electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles.
Is Britain following the EU?
The answer is partly, but the situation is more complicated than simply copying Brussels.
The European Commission proposed its Industrial Accelerator Act in March. The legislation would introduce “Made in EU” and low-carbon requirements for public procurement and public support in strategic sectors, including cars and batteries. It is designed to strengthen European manufacturing and reduce strategic dependencies on non-EU suppliers.
The proposal is not, however, a blanket ban on Chinese vehicles or a general import tariff.
The concern for Britain comes from the potential consequences for UK manufacturers and supply chains. The EU is considering rules that could favour European production when public money is involved. UK-built vehicles, batteries and components could potentially receive less favourable treatment unless Britain secures an appropriate relationship with the new framework.
The SMMT has warned that excluding Britain would damage an automotive sector that remains deeply integrated with Europe. Its analysis says UK automotive production directly supports €24 billion of economic activity in the EU and 250,000 jobs.
SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said: “Excluding the UK from ‘Made in Europe’ would be an own goal, weakening competitiveness, reducing scale and limiting consumer choice.”
The UK government is therefore seeking recognition as a “trusted partner” under the proposed EU arrangements.
There is another issue that matters even more immediately. From 1 January 2027, stricter rules of origin for electric vehicles under the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement are scheduled to apply. Vehicles that fail to meet the requirements could face a 10% tariff when traded between Britain and the EU.
This is separate from the Industrial Accelerator Act, but the two developments have become closely connected in the automotive sector.
Could Chinese EVs enter the EU through Britain?
This is one of Brussels’ concerns.
The EU has already imposed additional duties on Chinese battery electric vehicles following its investigation into Chinese government subsidies. The measures sit alongside the EU’s normal import duty and vary between manufacturers.
BYD faces a 17% countervailing duty, Geely 18.8% and SAIC 35.3%. Other cooperating manufacturers face 20.7%, while non-cooperating companies face 35.3%. The EU also applies its standard 10% import duty to these vehicles.
That means the effective EU tariff burden can reach about 45% for manufacturers subject to the highest additional duty.
Britain did not introduce equivalent measures. As a result, Chinese-built vehicles entering the UK face the standard UK tariff rather than an EU-style anti-subsidy duty.
That difference matters if the EU tightens its rules further. Brussels does not want Britain to become an easy route into the European market for vehicles that face substantially higher costs when entering the EU directly.
A Reuters report in September said the EU had urged Britain to raise tariffs on Chinese cars and align more closely with European trade policy. One EU official was quoted as saying: “A customs union would solve most of the problems of ‘made in Europe’.”
The UK government, however, has stressed that its trade policy will be determined independently.
Are Chinese manufacturers actually dumping cars?
This is perhaps the most important question.
“Dumping” has a specific meaning under trade law. It generally involves exporting goods at a price below their normal value, with evidence that this causes or threatens injury to domestic industry.
The EU has already concluded that Chinese BEV manufacturers benefit from government subsidies and that those subsidies threaten economic injury to European producers.
That does not automatically establish dumping in the UK.
In fact, the UK government confirmed in July that the independent Trade Remedies Authority had not initiated an investigation into Chinese electric vehicles. Ministers said Britain remained concerned about “overcapacity and underlying market distorting practices” but stressed that any action would have to serve UK industry.
That distinction is important. The rapid increase in Chinese vehicle registrations is clear evidence of competitive pressure, but high sales alone do not prove unlawful dumping.
Chinese manufacturers may also be winning customers because they offer competitive products at attractive prices. The September figures show that British buyers and fleet operators are responding strongly to that proposition.
What level could UK tariffs reach?
There is no confirmed UK tariff rate at present.
The most frequently discussed benchmark is the EU’s maximum effective rate of around 45%, combining the normal 10% import duty with the highest countervailing duty.
Reports suggest Britain could consider matching the EU approach. That does not necessarily mean every Chinese EV would attract a 45% tariff. A UK system could follow the EU model, with different rates according to manufacturer and the findings of a trade-remedies investigation.
The UK could therefore impose additional duties in the region of the EU’s 17% to 35.3% countervailing rates, on top of the existing 10% tariff. But any final figure would need to follow the UK’s own legal and economic assessment.
The government has already demonstrated that it is willing to use this mechanism. In August, the Trade Remedies Authority recommended provisional anti-dumping measures on Chinese boom lifts after finding that dumped imports had caused or were causing injury to UK industry.
That precedent suggests the UK has the machinery to act, but an automotive investigation would still require evidence.
What does this mean for fleets?
For fleet operators, tariffs could create both risks and opportunities.
Higher duties would probably increase the cost of affected Chinese-built vehicles, although manufacturers could absorb some of the increase to protect market share. Leasing companies and fleet buyers would also need to reassess whole-life costs, residual values and monthly rental rates.
There is also a wider question around competition.
Chinese manufacturers have helped accelerate the UK’s transition towards electrification by bringing more affordable EVs and PHEVs to the market. September’s figures demonstrate just how quickly customers are embracing that choice.
The government therefore faces a difficult balancing act. It wants to protect British automotive manufacturing and maintain access to the EU market without undermining competition or making electric vehicles less affordable.
For now, the key point is that Britain has not introduced tariffs on Chinese EVs. It is considering its options at a time when Chinese-owned brands are taking an increasingly large share of the UK market.
The eventual decision is likely to be shaped by three competing priorities: protecting UK automotive manufacturing, maintaining frictionless trade with Europe and keeping electric vehicles affordable for consumers and fleets.
The outcome could have a significant influence on Britain’s fleet market as the country moves towards its increasingly demanding zero-emission vehicle targets.

Yet another week of wavering vibes was capped off last week by action as a surprising jobs report reset expectations for the October Fed meeting.
Even though the mere 29,000 jobs added in September made for a "miss," the market celebrated what that meant: The labor market is definitely not overheating.
After Friday's gains for the stock market, the S&P 500 once again finished about where it had started the week as market forces continue to cancel each other out.
With a big week of jobs data behind us, the calendar of regularly scheduled programming will continue but leave plenty of space for organic news to grab the reins.
Taking point on the earnings calendar will be Tuesday's beverage production and distribution giant, Constellation Brands (STZ), followed by another check on the food & beverage business with PepsiCo (PEP) earnings on Thursday. While it's not often included in the discussion among AI's biggest names, data center operator Applied Digital's results will offer another check on the AI trade on Wednesday.
On the economic data front, the University of Michigan's twice-monthly survey of consumer sentiment is likely to capture the largest share of attention after the last reading of the index showed sentiment fell to levels below those seen during the 2008 financial crisis.
A cool jobs report puts the Fed on hold, economists say
In an abrupt turnaround from August's labor market outperformance, the US added just 29,000 jobs in September, missing expectations of 90,000, as the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%.
The release wasn't necessarily bad, argue BNP Paribas US economists Andrew Husby and James Egelhof. It just wasn't great.
"We see the broad trajectory of the US job market as positive, and consistent with our forecast of a gradually tightening trajectory we put in place in early June," the economists wrote to clients.
September's miss, economists say, points to a labor market that's continuing to lose steam amid a long period of "low hire, low fire" dynamics. Average hourly earnings rose an anemic 0.1% from August and are up 3% year over year, a level that's likely below the current rate of inflation.
What the jobs print is likely to do, though, is keep the Federal Reserve on hold in October. Odds of a 25 basis point hike at the FOMC's October meeting have pulled back to roughly 20%, per CME data, as a not-steaming-hot labor market reduces pressure to hike immediately.
"We remain optimistic on economic growth and hiring, owing to still-stimulative policy and very well embedded economic optimism," Husby and Egelhof wrote. "But that does not mean the Fed faces a hair-on-fire need to raise."

high_priority_articles.title: Apparel output contracts 7.4% in August even as textile production grows 13.1% - manufacturing.economictimes.indiatimes.com
high_priority_articles.summary: Apparel output contracts 7.4% in August even as textile production grows 13.1%  manufacturing.economictimes.indiatimes.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Wearing apparel production fell 5.6% cumulatively in April-August, contrasting with 11.9% growth in textiles, as export orders, global demand and trade uncertainties weigh on the downstream industry.
According to the Index of Industrial Production (IIP) released by the Statistics Ministry last week, overall growth in August 2026 stood at 8 per cent against 6.7 per cent in the preceding month.
Within the manufacturing sector, 18 of 23 industry groups have recorded positive growth in August 2026 over the year-ago month, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) said in a statement.
In contrast, the textile industry, which feeds apparel manufacturing, has recorded a strong growth of 13.1 per cent in August and a cumulative expansion of 11.9 per cent in the current fiscal year so far.
Among the constituents of the broader benchmark IIP, textile production weighs 3.27 points and wearing apparel 1.97 points on a scale of 100, which includes 76 points under 'Manufacturing'. Other industries such as 'Mining & Quarrying', 'Electricity & Gas Supply', and 'Water Supply, Sewerage & Waste Management' carry the remaining 24 points.
The gap between the production of upstream raw material manufacturers and the user industry in the downstream seems to be widening incessantly, irrespective of geopolitical situation, tariff uncertainties, and global macroeconomic conditions.
Explaining the divergent trend, A Sakthivel, Chairman of Apparel Export Promotion Council, said that the two indices cover different stages of production and therefore, "need not necessarily move in line with overall industrial output".
"Textile manufacturing largely covers upstream segments such as yarn and fabric, where production is influenced by raw-material prices, inventory and intermediate demand. Yarn prices, for instance, have seen a significant increase recently.
"Wearing apparel is the final, value-added stage and is more directly linked to export orders, buyer inventories and global retail demand. With the global environment currently marked by geopolitical and trade uncertainties, apparel production can therefore respond more quickly to changes in external demand," he said.
India's textile and apparel industry has a strong domestic demand base alongside its export orientation. According to the Ministry of Textiles' National Household Survey 2024, the overall textile market was estimated at Rs 14.95 lakh crore, of which the domestic market accounted for Rs 12.02 lakh crore - roughly 80 per cent.
India also aims to increase its apparel exports to USD 40 billion by 2030 from around USD 16 billion at present.
Moving back and forth
The barometer shows that the manufacturing of wearing apparel last year slipped by 2 per cent in September and over 7.3 per cent in October before rising 6.7 per cent in November and over 17 per cent in December. This year, the index recorded a sharp fall of 8.6 per cent in January followed by another 3.4 per cent decline in February.
What is more concerning is that a month after the outbreak of the US-Iran war, the index rose in March by 4.8 per cent sequentially but fell over 10 per cent in April.
During May and June, the index showed a growth of 3.6 per cent and 2.3 per cent. However, it contracted again in July and August by 2.3 per cent and 7.2 per cent, respectively.
At the same time, textile production logged steady growth month-on-month between August and December last year, except for a one-time fall of 7.7 pc in October 2025. This year, textile production saw a significant drop only in January (5.7 per cent) and February (24.2 per cent). However, it rebounded sharply by 48 per cent in March and stayed at the same level until August this year, notwithstanding the unstable geopolitical situation and unabated global trade disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz.
Broader impact
According to the National Accounts Statistics 2025, the textile and apparel sector accounts for around 2 per cent of the country's GDP and 11 per cent of manufacturing GVA (Gross Value Added) on average over the last three years.
"A prolonged contraction in apparel manufacturing could affect manufacturing, value addition, exports, investment and employment, with implications for overall economic activity," Sakthivel added.
According to industry players, the apparel industry continues to show resilience. Apparel exports were down 9.1 per cent during April-August 2026-27, reflecting the challenging global environment, but the pace of decline has moderated in recent months.
"The industry is also actively diversifying markets through new FTAs (free trade agreements) and expanding market access, while the upcoming festive season is expected to support demand. Thus, the current IIP numbers merit close monitoring, but they should be seen as reflecting the adjustment of a globally integrated, value-added industry to changing market conditions rather than as a broad-based deterioration in the sector," the AEPC chairman said.
Despite challenges, apparel manufacturers, as well as exporters, are betting big on the upcoming festive demands from overseas and expect sales to pick up in the next couple of months.
Experts said that new FTAs and expanding market access are opening opportunities for market diversification, while India's large domestic market, particularly with festive-season demand, provides an additional source of support.
They said that with the industry's ability to adapt to changing global conditions, apparel manufacturing is expected to regain momentum and contribute positively to India's growth going forward.
"The manufacturing growth is slow, but it is cyclical. The growth will pick up in two to three months. We are making Christmas orders at present," said Sharad Saraf, a Mumbai-based exporter and CMD of Technocraft Industries.
Saraf, who also has a textile unit in Amravati, Maharashtra, said the manufacturing units need a skilled workforce permanently and must hire additional workers from time to time depending on the order book.

high_priority_articles.title: 2034 World Cup: Saudi Arabia puts $2.5bn NEOM stadium on hold amid infrastructure review - businessday.ng
high_priority_articles.summary: 2034 World Cup: Saudi Arabia puts $2.5bn NEOM stadium on hold amid infrastructure review  businessday.ng
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia has put plans for a $2.5 billion stadium intended to host matches at the 2034 FIFA World Cup on hold, as the kingdom evaluates some of its ambitious projects under its Vision 2030 economic diversification programme.
The 46,000-seat NEOM Stadium, planned as one of the tournament’s venues, is listed as on hold with no completion date in data from MEED Projects, according to Reuters. Two sources familiar with the project also said plans to build the stadium had been shelved indefinitely.
The futuristic venue was designed to be built about 350 metres above ground within The Line, a 160 kilometer steel-and-glass development that forms part of the wider NEOM project.
Saudi Arabia was officially named host of the 2034 FIFA World Cup after its bid was ratified by acclamation on December 11, 2024, at an Extraordinary FIFA Congress in Zurich, Switzerland. The kingdom was the sole bidding candidate.
Read Also: FIFA confirms Saudi Arabia as host for 2034 World Cup amid controversy
The tournament will be the third men’s FIFA World Cup hosted in the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) region, after South Korea and Japan in 2002 and Qatar in 2022. It will also be the first 48-team World Cup hosted by a single nation.
NEOM project faces reprioritisation
The decision comes as Saudi Arabia reassesses some of its largest development projects under Vision 2030, an ambitious programme aimed at diversifying the economy and reducing its dependence on oil.
Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of the Public Investment Fund, which owns NEOM, said in April that The Line was no longer a priority and was not essential to deliver before 2030, although he denied that projects had been cancelled.
The NEOM Stadium was originally conceived as an elevated arena within The Line and formed part of Saudi Arabia’s plans to showcase the kingdom’s futuristic infrastructure during the World Cup.
NEOM and the Saudi government’s media office did not respond to requests for comment on the stadium. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Sports referred questions to the World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority.
The authority said substantial construction milestones for the tournament were already being delivered but did not directly address the NEOM Stadium or its reported cost.
$22.7bn World Cup infrastructure programme
Saudi Arabia plans to stage the tournament across five host cities; Riyadh, Jeddah, Al Khobar, Abha and NEOM.
The kingdom plans to build or renovate 15 stadiums across the five cities, comprising 10 new venues and five major renovations, alongside major transport and infrastructure projects. MEED Projects estimates the total value of World Cup-related projects at $22.7 billion.
Despite the NEOM Stadium being put on hold, other major venues are progressing. The Prince Mohammed Bin Salman Stadium in Qiddiya, for example, has advanced with major construction and recently secured a $221 million mechanical, electrical and plumbing contract.
Saudi Arabia’s 2034 World Cup is a major component of its global sports strategy, which has seen the Public Investment Fund invest heavily in football and other sports as part of Vision 2030.
Financial and geopolitical pressures
The decision to put the NEOM Stadium on hold comes amid wider financial and geopolitical pressures facing the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia is dealing with disruptions to energy shipments and security risks linked to the regional conflict, including attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces, while weaker oil activity has added pressure to the economy.
Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Finance expects a wider fiscal deficit and a 3.6 percent contraction in real GDP this year.
The developments have increased scrutiny of the kingdom’s spending commitments under Vision 2030, particularly its large-scale giga-projects designed to transform the economy and reduce its reliance on oil.
The World Cup remains a major pillar of that strategy, with Saudi Arabia continuing to invest in football infrastructure even as some of its most ambitious development projects are delayed, downsised or reprioritised.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
05 October 2026
The plan to build a stadium that would have been a centrepiece for the 2034 FIFA World Cup in Saudi Arabia is being “quietly shelved”, according to a report.
Citing unnamed sources, Reuters said that the 46,000-capacity Neom Stadium, originally billed as an elevated glass arena in the 160km-long vertical city The Line, has been “shelved indefinitely”.
The Line itself has been significantly reduced in scope and in April this year, Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of the Kingdom’s Public Investment Fund, which owns Neom, confirmed that The Line is no longer a priority and was not vital before its original delivery target of 2030, although he denied any projects had been cancelled.
Saudi Arabia’s World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority told Reuters that “substantial delivery” of construction milestones for the event was already taking place but did not address questions around the Neom stadium and costs. Meanwhile, Neom and the Saudi government media office did not reply to requests for comment.
Neom was established as a special economic zone under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030, a plan that aims to diversify the economy in the Kingdom and reduce its reliance on oil.
But last year, the PIF moved from focusing on expensive gigaprojects to a strategy supporting projects with a more immediate financial return.
In January, Reuters reported that construction of a huge cube-shaped structure called the Mukaab, at the heart of Riyadh’s New Murabba development, had been suspended.
But work on other stadiums that are either being refurbished or newly constructed continues, including the Aramco Stadium in the eastern city of Al Khobar, which will be completed by the end of this year.

high_priority_articles.title: China Railway Construction Engineering Pivots to Tanzania Dira 2050 Vision After Decades of Infrastructure Development - streamlinefeed.co.ke
high_priority_articles.summary: China Railway Construction Engineering Pivots to Tanzania Dira 2050 Vision After Decades of Infrastructure Development  streamlinefeed.co.ke
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The strategic pivot was highlighted at the Phoenix Global Development Forum for Enterprises in Dar es Salaam, where government officials, business leaders, and academics convened to map the next phase of Sino-Tanzanian economic cooperation. For CRJE, the forum marked a transition from historical aid-driven projects to modern, commercial infrastructure development aligned with Tanzania's long-term economic blueprint.
From TAZARA to Modern Infrastructure
The company's Tanzanian footprint dates back to 1969, when its parent group, China Railway Construction Engineering Group (CRCEG), dispatched 1,114 employees to participate in the construction of TAZARA. This monumental infrastructure project was designed to link landlocked Zambia's copper belt to the Tanzanian port of Dar es Salaam, bypassing routes controlled by apartheid-era regimes in southern Africa.
During the initial construction phase, the Chinese team undertook approximately 506,400 square meters of building works along the railway line. This extensive effort included the construction of 93 stations, locomotive and rolling stock repair plants, technical training schools, depots, hospitals, and accommodation facilities. The project not only transformed regional logistics but also established a deep cultural and technical exchange between the two nations.
After TAZARA became operational, CRCEG retained a specialized team to undertake ongoing maintenance work along the railway corridor. The company formally registered its Tanzanian branch in Dar es Salaam in 2000, coinciding with the country's launch of Vision 2025. In 2013, as its business portfolio expanded beyond rail, the entity was rebranded as CRJE (East Africa) Limited, reflecting its broader mandate in the regional construction market.
Aligning with Dira 2050
Tanzania's newly articulated National Development Vision 2050, popularly known as Dira 2050, demands massive upgrades in transport, energy, and urban infrastructure to achieve middle-to-high-income economic status. The Phoenix Global Development Forum, co-organized by Phoenix TV and the Chinese Enterprises Association in Tanzania (CEAT), provided a platform for CRJE to outline its aspirations for this next developmental chapter.
The forum was attended by high-profile figures, including Minister of State in the President's Office for Planning and Investment, Prof Kitila Mkumbo, and United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Resident Representative Shigeki Komatsubara. Their presence underscored the institutional importance placed on foreign direct investment and public-private partnerships in realizing the nation's mid-century goals.
For CRJE, the transition to Dira 2050 involves moving beyond traditional civil works to encompass complex, technology-driven infrastructure projects. This includes modern port expansions, smart city developments, and large-scale irrigation schemes designed to support Tanzania's rapidly growing population and agricultural export ambitions. The company views its historical presence as a unique competitive advantage, offering institutional memory and established government relations that newer market entrants lack.
The Evolution of Sino-Tanzanian Cooperation
The trajectory of CRJE mirrors the broader evolution of Sino-African economic relations. In the 1970s, projects like TAZARA were primarily state-led aid initiatives, funded by concessional loans and driven by geopolitical solidarity. Today, the partnership is characterized by commercial contracts, joint ventures, and a focus on mutual economic benefit.
A critical component of this modern partnership is technology transfer and local capacity building. Echoing the technical training schools established during the TAZARA era, CRJE now emphasizes the employment and upskilling of Tanzanian engineers and project managers. This approach not only reduces operational costs but also fosters local goodwill and ensures that the technical expertise required to maintain complex infrastructure remains within the country.
Challenges and Future Prospects
Despite its deep roots, CRJE operates in an increasingly competitive and scrutinized market. Tanzanian authorities are placing greater emphasis on debt sustainability, environmental compliance, and the use of local subcontractors. International financial institutions and domestic civil society organizations frequently demand greater transparency regarding the terms of infrastructure financing and the long-term economic viability of mega-projects.
Furthermore, the company must navigate the complexities of Tanzania's evolving regulatory environment, which seeks to maximize local content and ensure that foreign investments translate into tangible job creation and skills development. As Tanzania pushes toward its mid-century economic goals, CRJE's evolution from a railway builder to a comprehensive infrastructure partner reflects the maturing, complex nature of foreign direct investment in East Africa. The success of this transition will depend on the firm's ability to balance commercial imperatives with the developmental priorities of its host nation.
Industry observers note that the next decade will be critical for CRJE as it competes against both Western contractors and other Asian firms for lucrative government tenders. To maintain its market leadership, the firm is increasingly integrating green building practices and renewable energy components into its project proposals, aligning with global climate finance requirements. Ultimately, CRJE's continued relevance in Tanzania will be measured not just by the volume of concrete poured, but by its contribution to sustainable, inclusive economic growth under the Dira 2050 framework.

high_priority_articles.title: Brussels Sets the New Customs Codes Ahead of the EUDR Rollout - woodcentral.com.au
high_priority_articles.summary: Brussels Sets the New Customs Codes Ahead of the EUDR Rollout  woodcentral.com.au
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The European Commission has firmed up its customs codes in the weeks leading up to the EUDR rollout, with timber shipped into the 27-nation bloc from 30 December requiring a due diligence statement upon entry. That is according to the Commission’s deforestation team, which released the updated TARIC document for the EU Deforestation Regulation late last month and is poised to start a new round of online training later today.
“If the obligations are not met, import or export is prohibited,” the Commission’s customs directorate states in the document’s first edition, with code C716 telling customs that the company declaring the goods holds a due diligence statement for them. A container of sawn timber therefore takes the same code as a shipment of coffee, and timber leaving the EU takes it as well as timber arriving.
It comes as Brussels hands every statement to the national authority of the EU country where the operator is based from 15 October, under Implementing Regulation 2026/1565, with exporters outside the bloc assigned to a member state through their registration. Once a statement’s reference number reaches the company that lodged it, no authority can reject the statement, and that number is the one quoted beside the code.
Meanwhile, global exporters that clear their own timber into the EU are considered upstream operators under the Commission’s roles guidance and need a valid EU EORI number and registration in the system before they can lodge a statement. The first European company to sell that timber on is an operator too, so the same shipment needs two statements before it reaches a buyer.
Elsewhere on the declaration, customs now has codes for re-imports, samples, goods placed on the market before the rules apply, and a downstream company exporting goods already covered by a statement. Used goods and packing have their own codes too, following the carve-outs Brussels wrote into the product list, which removed used timber, bamboo, and loaded pallets from the regulation last month.
Under last December’s amendment, an importer’s first buyer keeps the reference number on file for at least five years and never passes it on, ending the forwarding of numbers down the chain that Austria’s sawmillers had warned would run into the hundreds of thousands. Large downstream operators and traders still register in the system, whilst smaller firms downstream only keep their records and report any product they suspect does not comply.
“With this package, we are providing the clarity and predictability that businesses, Member States and our international partners need,” Jessika Roswall, the European Commissioner for Environment, said in July when she adopted the system rules alongside the product list. The Commission runs the first of three online sessions for upstream operators today, with three more for micro and small primary producers on their one-off simplified declaration.
As it stands, large and medium operators must comply from 30 December, joined by micro and small firms already covered by the old EU Timber Regulation. Only a statement lodged on the system’s production server counts for customs, whilst its acceptance server takes practice statements that have no legal value.

high_priority_articles.title: South Korea's AI Chip Boom Deepens Economic Concentration Risk - briefasia.com
high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea's AI Chip Boom Deepens Economic Concentration Risk  briefasia.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Export Engine Narrows
South Korea's economy is riding an artificial intelligence wave, but the prosperity is landing in fewer hands than before. The country's semiconductor industry has captured a disproportionate share of growth as global demand for high-bandwidth memory chips accelerates, creating a structural vulnerability that policymakers have struggled to address for years.
The concentration is most visible in trade figures. Memory chips now account for an expanding portion of South Korea's total exports, with a small group of manufacturers capturing nearly all the gains. SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dominate high-bandwidth memory production, the specialised components that power AI data centres and training systems. As hyperscalers in the United States and China race to expand computing capacity, orders have poured into these two firms at volumes that dwarf growth elsewhere in the economy.
This dynamic reverses an earlier trend. A decade ago, South Korean industrial policy emphasised diversification away from electronics hardware. Successive governments launched initiatives to build strength in biotechnology, renewable energy equipment, and electric vehicle components. Those efforts yielded modest results, but none generated export revenues on the scale that memory chips deliver today. The AI boom has effectively re-anchored the economy to semiconductor cyclicality, just as officials were attempting to reduce that exposure.
Labour Market Distortions
The chipmaker windfall is reshaping employment patterns in ways that worry labour economists. High-value manufacturing jobs are concentrating in semiconductor hubs around Icheon, Pyeongtaek, and Cheongju, where SK Hynix and Samsung operate advanced fabrication plants. Wages in these facilities have climbed faster than the national average, pulling engineering talent away from smaller manufacturers and research institutions.
Meanwhile, export-oriented industries outside semiconductors face stagnant demand. Shipbuilding orders remain below pre-pandemic levels. Petrochemical producers are losing margin to Middle Eastern competitors with cheaper feedstock. Steel mills are cutting capacity as Chinese supply floods regional markets. The result is a two-tier labour market in which semiconductor engineers command premium compensation while workers in legacy industries face wage stagnation or redundancy.
This disparity complicates monetary policy. The Bank of Korea must balance inflation pressures in semiconductor regions against deflationary trends in industrial cities dependent on older export sectors. Interest rate decisions that cool overheating in Gyeonggi Province can deepen recessions in Ulsan or Pohang.
Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
Concentration in memory chips also amplifies geopolitical risk. South Korea produces roughly 60 per cent of global DRAM and a similar share of NAND flash, the two dominant memory technologies. That market position makes the country indispensable to the AI supply chain, but it also creates a single point of failure. Any disruption to production - whether from natural disaster, equipment failure, or cross-strait military tension - would cascade through global technology markets.
Policymakers in Seoul recognise the risk but have limited tools to mitigate it. Efforts to attract foreign chipmakers have produced modest investment from Intel and TSMC, yet neither company plans to manufacture leading-edge memory in South Korea. The country's competitive advantage remains tied to the incumbents. Attempts to diversify into logic chips face entrenched competition from Taiwan and, increasingly, from subsidised fabs in the United States and Europe under industrial policy programmes that explicitly aim to reduce dependence on Asian suppliers.
Policy Inertia
The concentration challenge is not new, but the AI boom has made it more acute. Government officials have floated proposals to redirect semiconductor profits into venture funds supporting adjacent industries, or to impose investment requirements on chipmakers similar to those in battery manufacturing. None have advanced beyond discussion stages. The political economy of intervention is difficult: Samsung and SK Hynix are among the largest employers and taxpayers in the country, and their export performance underpins macroeconomic stability. Policies that constrain their operations risk immediate GDP contraction for uncertain long-term gains.
At the same time, younger firms struggle to access capital. Venture funding in South Korea remains heavily skewed toward e-commerce and consumer internet platforms, sectors with lower capital requirements and faster exit timelines. Deep-tech startups in materials science, photonics, or biotechnology face a shallow investor base and limited government procurement support. The gap between semiconductor incumbents and potential competitors is widening, not closing.
South Korea's economy is growing, but the gains are accruing in a narrower band than at any point in recent decades. The AI chip boom has delivered a revenue surge, yet it has also locked the country deeper into a dependency it spent years trying to escape. Whether that trade-off proves sustainable will depend on how long the current memory cycle lasts - and what comes after.
